chapters.title: Book IV: Three Love Problems — Chapter XXXVIII
paragraphs:
“C’est beaucoup que le jugement des hommes sur les actions humaines;
tôt ou tard il devient efficace.”—GUIZOT.

Sir James Chettam found nothing to approve of in Mr. Brooke’s new activities, but disapproval was easier than prevention. One day, arriving alone to have lunch with the Cadwalladers, Sir James explained why he had come without his wife—
“I can’t speak to you freely with Celia there: it might hurt her feelings. Really, it wouldn’t be right.”

“I know what you mean—the ‘Pioneer’ at the Grange!” Mrs. Cadwallader broke in before her friend had quite finished. “It’s dreadful, this new habit of buying whistles and blowing them where everyone can hear. Staying in bed all day playing dominoes, like poor Lord Plessy, would at least be private, and easier to bear.”

“I see the ‘Trumpet’ has started attacking our friend Brooke,” said the Rector, leaning back with the same comfortable smile he would have worn if the attacks had been directed at himself. “Some tremendous sarcasm about a landlord within easy reach of Middlemarch who collects his own rents and gives nothing back.”
“I do wish Brooke would stop doing that,” Sir James said, his brow contracting in a small, irritated frown.

“But is he actually going to stand for election?” asked Mr. Cadwallader. “I saw Farebrother yesterday. He leans towards the Whigs himself, waves the flag for Brougham and Useful Knowledge; that’s the worst I can say of him. He tells me Brooke is building up quite a following. His chief supporter is Bulstrode the banker. Still, Farebrother thinks Brooke would fare badly at the nomination.”

“Exactly,” Sir James said earnestly. “I’ve been making inquiries. I never knew anything about Middlemarch politics before: the county has always been my concern. Brooke is relying on their throwing Oliver out because he supports Peel. But Hawley tells me that if they put forward a Whig, it’s bound to be Bagster—one of those candidates from heaven knows where, but firmly against the Ministers and an experienced man in Parliament. Hawley is rather rough; he forgot whom he was talking to. He said that if Brooke wanted people to throw things at him, there were cheaper ways than taking to the election platform.”
“I warned you all,” said Mrs. Cadwallader, spreading her hands. “Long ago I told Humphrey that Mr. Brooke was heading for a splash in the mud. And now he’s made it.”
“Well, he might have decided to marry,” the Rector observed. “That would have landed him in a more serious mess than a little flirtation with politics.”
“He may do that next,” Mrs. Cadwallader replied, “once he’s emerged from the mud with a fever.”

“It’s his own dignity that concerns me most,” said Sir James. “Naturally the family connection makes me care all the more. But he’s getting older, and I hate to think of him exposing himself like this. They’ll dig up everything they can against him.”
“I suppose persuasion would be useless,” said the Rector. “Brooke combines stubbornness and changeability in such a peculiar way. Have you tried talking to him about it?”

“Well, no,” Sir James admitted. “I’m reluctant to seem to be giving orders. But I’ve talked to young Ladislaw, whom Brooke is turning into his general assistant. Ladislaw seems clever enough to do anything. I thought I should hear his views, and he’s against Brooke standing this time. I think he’ll bring him round; I think we may put off the nomination.”
“I understand,” said Mrs. Cadwallader, nodding. “The independent candidate hasn’t learned his speeches properly yet.”

“But Ladislaw—there’s another tiresome business,” Sir James continued. “We’ve had him to dinner at the Hall two or three times—you’ve met him, by the way—as Brooke’s guest and Casaubon’s relation, thinking he was only paying a short visit. Now I find all Middlemarch talking about him as the editor of the ‘Pioneer.’ Stories are circulating about a foreign scribbler, an emissary from abroad, and all the rest.”
“Casaubon won’t care for that,” said the Rector.
“Ladislaw does have some foreign ancestry,” Sir James replied. “I hope he doesn’t take up extreme views and drag Brooke along with him.”

“Oh, that Mr. Ladislaw is a dangerous young fellow,” said Mrs. Cadwallader, “with his opera songs and his quick tongue. A kind of Byronic hero—a romantic conspirator, I should say. And Thomas Aquinas isn’t fond of him. I could see that when the picture was brought over.”

“I’m reluctant to raise the subject with Casaubon,” said Sir James. “He has more right to intervene than I do. But the whole affair is disagreeable. What a role for anyone with respectable connections to put himself in! One of those newspaper men! Just look at Keck, who runs the ‘Trumpet.’ I saw him with Hawley the other day. His articles are sound enough, I believe, but he’s such a vulgar fellow that I wished he supported the other side.”

“What else can you expect from these petty Middlemarch newspapers?” asked the Rector. “I doubt you could find a man of much standing anywhere to promote interests he doesn’t really care about, for wages that scarcely keep his elbows covered.”
“Exactly. That’s why it’s so irritating that Brooke should place a man with a connection of sorts to the family in such a position. Personally, I think Ladislaw rather foolish to accept it.”
“It’s Aquinas’s fault,” said Mrs. Cadwallader. “Why didn’t he use his connections to get Ladislaw an attaché’s post, or send him to India? That’s how families dispose of troublesome young branches.”
“There’s no telling how far the trouble may spread,” Sir James said anxiously. “But if Casaubon says nothing, what am I to do?”

“My dear Sir James,” said the Rector, “let’s not make too much of it. Very likely the whole thing will amount to nothing. In a month or two Brooke and young Master Ladislaw will tire of each other. Ladislaw will fly away, Brooke will sell the ‘Pioneer,’ and everything will return to normal.”

“We have one good hope: he won’t enjoy feeling his money trickle away,” said Mrs. Cadwallader. “If I had an itemized list of election costs, I could frighten him. Grand words like Expenditure are no use. I wouldn’t lecture him on bloodletting; I’d empty a pot of leeches over him. What we good, stingy people dislike is having our sixpences sucked out of us.”

“And he won’t enjoy having his faults dragged into the open,” said Sir James. “There’s his management of the estate. They’ve already started on that. It really pains me to see it; the trouble is right under our noses. I do think a man has a duty to do his best for his land and tenants, particularly in such hard times.”

“Perhaps the ‘Trumpet’ will stir him into changing things, and some good will come of the affair,” said the Rector. “I’d certainly welcome it. There would be less grumbling when my tithe was paid. I don’t know how I’d manage if Tipton didn’t have a fixed payment in place of the tithe.”

“I want him to employ a competent man to look after the place. I want him to take Garth back,” said Sir James. “He dismissed Garth twelve years ago, and things have gone downhill ever since. I’m considering having Garth manage my own estate: he’s drawn up such an excellent plan for my buildings, and Lovegood isn’t quite equal to the work. But Garth wouldn’t take on Tipton again unless Brooke gave him complete control.”

“And quite right too,” said the Rector. “Garth is an independent man, original and straightforward. Once, while doing a valuation for me, he told me plainly that clergymen rarely understood business and did harm when they interfered. Yet he said it as calmly and respectfully as though he were discussing sailors. He’d transform the parish of Tipton if Brooke let him manage it. I wish you could bring that about with help from the ‘Trumpet.’”

“If Dorothea had stayed close to her uncle, there might have been a chance,” said Sir James. “In time she might have gained some influence over him, and she was always troubled about the estate. She had remarkably good ideas on such matters. Now Casaubon occupies her completely. Celia complains about it a good deal. Since his attack, we can scarcely persuade her to dine with us.” Sir James finished with a look combining pity and disgust. Mrs. Cadwallader shrugged, as if to say that she, at least, was unlikely to find anything surprising in that quarter.
“Poor Casaubon!” said the Rector. “It was a nasty attack. He looked broken when I saw him at the Archdeacon’s the other day.”
“The fact is,” Sir James resumed, choosing not to dwell on these attacks, “Brooke wishes his tenants no harm, or anyone else. But he’s fallen into this habit of shaving a little off every expense.”
“Well, that’s a blessing,” said Mrs. Cadwallader. “It helps him recognize himself in the morning. He may not know his own opinions, but he knows his own pocket.”
“I don’t believe a man saves money by being stingy with his land,” said Sir James.

“Oh, stinginess can be abused like any other virtue. Keeping your own pigs thin won’t do,” said Mrs. Cadwallader, who had stood up to look through the window. “But speak of an independent politician, and here he comes.”
“What! Brooke?” her husband asked.
“Yes. Now, Humphrey, you work on him with the ‘Trumpet,’ and I’ll apply the leeches. What will you do, Sir James?”

“The truth is, with our relationship, I dislike being the one to bring it up with Brooke. It’s all so unpleasant. I do wish people would conduct themselves like gentlemen,” said the good baronet, feeling that this was a simple and comprehensive scheme for society’s welfare.

“So here you all are, eh?” said Mr. Brooke, shuffling from one to the other and shaking hands. “I meant to go up to the Hall later, Chettam. Pleasant to find everyone together, though, you know. Well, what do you make of things? Moving rather fast! Lafitte was right when he said, ‘Since yesterday, a century has passed away.’ Across the water they’re already in the next century, you know. Moving faster than we are.”
“Indeed they are,” said the Rector, picking up the newspaper. “The ‘Trumpet’ accuses you of falling behind. Have you seen it?”
“Eh? No,” said Mr. Brooke. He dropped his gloves into his hat and hurriedly adjusted his eyeglass. But Mr. Cadwallader held on to the paper, and said with amusement in his eyes—

“Look at this! It’s all about a landlord not far from Middlemarch who collects his own rents. They call him the most backward-looking man in the county—‘retrogressive.’ I think they must have learned that word from your ‘Pioneer.’”

“Oh, that’s Keck—an ignorant fellow, you know. Retrogressive, indeed! Excellent. He thinks it means destructive. They want to paint me as a destroyer, you know,” said Mr. Brooke, buoyed by the cheerfulness an opponent’s supposed ignorance usually supplies.

“I think he understands the word. Here are a few sharp jabs. _If asked to describe a man who is retrogressive in the worst sense, we would name someone who calls himself a reformer of our constitution while allowing everything directly under his charge to decay: a philanthropist who cannot bear to see one scoundrel hanged, yet lets five honest tenants half starve; a man who screams about corruption while charging crushing rents; who bellows himself red over rotten boroughs, yet accepts a rotten gate in every field on his farms. No doubt he is wonderfully generous towards Leeds and Manchester: he would give them any number of representatives, provided those gentlemen paid for their seats themselves. What he objects to giving is a little rent money back to help a tenant buy livestock, or money for repairs to keep the weather out of a tenant’s barn, or to make his home look less like an Irish peasant’s hut. But we all know the joker’s definition of a philanthropist: a man whose charity grows in proportion to the square of the distance._ And so it continues. The rest explains what kind of lawmaker such a philanthropist would be,” the Rector concluded. He dropped the paper, clasped his hands behind his head, and regarded Mr. Brooke with amused impartiality.

“Well, that’s rather good, you know,” said Mr. Brooke, picking up the paper. He tried to take the attack as lightly as his neighbour, but his colour rose and his smile was nervous. “That bit about bellowing himself red over rotten boroughs—I’ve never made a speech about rotten boroughs in my life. And all this bellowing myself red—these men don’t understand good satire. Satire ought to be true up to a point, you know. I remember reading that somewhere in ‘The Edinburgh.’ It must be true up to a point.”

“But the remark about the gates does hit home,” said Sir James, anxious to proceed delicately. “Dagley told me the other day he hadn’t a decent gate anywhere on his farm. Garth has designed a new kind. I wish you’d try it. A man ought to put some of his timber to that use.”
“You like fancy farming, Chettam, you know,” said Mr. Brooke, apparently scanning the ‘Trumpet’s’ columns. “That’s your hobby, and you don’t object to paying for it.”

“I thought standing for Parliament was the most expensive hobby in existence,” said Mrs. Cadwallader. “They said the last man who failed at Middlemarch—wasn’t he called Giles?—spent ten thousand pounds and lost because he hadn’t spent enough on bribes. What a bitter thought to live with!”
“Someone was saying,” the Rector added with a laugh, “that for bribery East Retford couldn’t begin to compare with Middlemarch.”

“Nothing of the sort,” said Mr. Brooke. “It’s the Tories who bribe, you know. Hawley and his people buy men drinks—hot codlings and that sort of thing—and take voters to the poll drunk. But they won’t have everything their own way from now on—not in future, you know. I admit Middlemarch is a little backward; the freemen are a little backward. But we’ll educate them, bring them forward, you know. The best people there support us.”
“Hawley says some of your supporters will hurt your chances,” Sir James remarked. “He says Bulstrode the banker will do you harm.”

“And if they throw things at you,” Mrs. Cadwallader put in, “half the rotten eggs will express their hatred of your committee member. Good heavens! Imagine being pelted for holding the wrong opinions. And wasn’t there a story about a man they pretended to carry triumphantly in a chair, only to drop him deliberately into a rubbish heap!”

“Being pelted is nothing beside having your faults exposed,” said the Rector. “That’s what I’d fear if we parsons had to win advancement on an election platform. I’d dread their adding up all my days spent fishing. Honestly, I believe truth is the hardest thing anyone can throw at you.”
“The point is,” said Sir James, “a man who enters public life must expect the consequences. He must put himself beyond the reach of slander.”

“My dear Chettam, that sounds very fine, you know,” Mr. Brooke replied. “But how do you protect yourself against slander? Read history—consider ostracism, persecution, martyrdom, and so forth. They always happen to the best men. But what’s that line in Horace? _Fiat justitia, ruat_ … something or other.”
“Exactly,” said Sir James, rather more heatedly than usual. “By being safe from slander I mean being able to point to the facts and disprove it.”
“And paying the bills you have chosen to run up yourself hardly makes you a martyr,” Mrs. Cadwallader added.

It was Sir James’s obvious irritation, however, that affected Mr. Brooke most. “Well, Chettam, you know,” he said, rising, taking his hat and leaning on his stick, “you and I follow different systems. With your farms you believe in spending freely. I don’t claim my own system works in every circumstance—in every circumstance, you understand.”
“Rents ought to be reassessed from time to time,” said Sir James. “An occasional rebate is all very well, but I prefer a fair valuation. What do you think, Cadwallader?”

“I agree. In Brooke’s place I’d silence the ‘Trumpet’ immediately: get Garth to revalue the farms and give him a free hand over gates and repairs. That’s my assessment of the political situation,” said the Rector. He hooked his thumbs into his armholes, making himself look broader, and laughed towards Mr. Brooke.

“That would look very grand, you know,” said Mr. Brooke. “But name another landlord who has seized his tenants’ property for unpaid rent as rarely as I have. I keep the old tenants on. I’m extraordinarily easy with them, I assure you, extraordinarily easy. I have my own ideas and stand by them. A man who does that always gets called eccentric, inconsistent, and so on. When I alter my course, it will be according to my own ideas.”
At that point Mr. Brooke remembered a parcel he had forgotten to send from the Grange, and hurriedly said goodbye to everyone.

“I didn’t mean to presume with Brooke,” said Sir James. “I can see he’s irritated. But whatever he says about keeping old tenants, the truth is that no new tenant would take those farms on the present terms.”

“I fancy he’ll come round eventually,” said the Rector. “But Elinor, you were pulling against us. You wanted to frighten him out of spending, while we wanted to frighten him into it. Better let him try to win popularity and discover that his reputation as a landlord blocks the way. I don’t think the ‘Pioneer,’ or Ladislaw, or Brooke making speeches to Middlemarch matters two straws. What matters is whether the people of Tipton parish can live comfortably.”

“Excuse me, but you two took the wrong approach,” said Mrs. Cadwallader. “You should have shown him how bad management costs him money; then we’d all have been pulling together. If you mount him on the horse of politics, I warn you what may happen. Riding sticks at home and calling them ideas was harmless enough.”

chapters.title: Book IV: Three Love Problems — Chapter XXXIX
paragraphs:
“If, as I have, you also doe,
Vertue attired in woman see,
And dare love that, and say so too,
And forget the He and She;

And if this love, though placed so,
From prophane men you hide,
Which will no faith on this bestow,
Or, if they doe, deride:

Then you have done a braver thing
Than all the Worthies did,
And a braver thence will spring,
Which is, to keep that hid.”
—DR. DONNE.

Sir James Chettam was not inventive, but his growing wish to bring pressure on Brooke, combined with his lasting faith in Dorothea’s influence, finally produced a small scheme. He would use Celia’s feeling unwell as a reason to fetch Dorothea alone to the Hall. On the way, after explaining the whole situation concerning her uncle’s management of his estate, he would leave her at the Grange with the carriage.
And so, one afternoon near four, as Mr. Brooke and Ladislaw sat in the library, the door opened and Mrs. Casaubon was announced.

A moment earlier Will had been sunk in boredom. Obliged to help Mr. Brooke arrange “documents” on hanging sheep-stealers, he was demonstrating the mind’s ability to ride several horses at once: inwardly he was planning to find lodgings in Middlemarch and end his continual residence at the Grange. Through these more settled thoughts flickered the amusing vision of an epic about sheep-stealing, written with Homer’s wealth of detail. At the announcement of Mrs. Casaubon he sprang up as though shocked by electricity, his fingertips tingling. Anyone watching would have noticed a change in his colour, in the set of his face, in the brightness of his eyes, as if every particle of his body had relayed news of a magical touch. And it had. Magic that works is nature surpassing itself. Who can measure the delicacy of those impressions that carry the character of a soul as well as a body? They make a man’s passion for one woman differ from his passion for another as delight in morning light over a valley, river and white mountain summit differs from delight among Chinese lanterns and glass panels. Will, moreover, was exceptionally responsive. A skilfully drawn violin bow nearby could change the whole appearance of the world for him in a stroke; his outlook shifted as readily as his mood. Dorothea’s arrival brought the freshness of morning.
“Well, my dear, what a pleasure,” said Mr. Brooke, coming forward to kiss her. “Left Casaubon with his books, I suppose? Quite right. We mustn’t let you grow too learned for a woman, you know.”

“No danger of that, uncle,” Dorothea said. She turned and shook Will’s hand with frank good humour, offering no other greeting before continuing her answer to her uncle. “I learn very slowly. When I mean to concentrate on books, my thoughts often run off to play. Becoming learned isn’t nearly as easy as planning cottages.”
She sat beside her uncle, opposite Will, plainly absorbed in something that almost drove him from her attention. He felt absurdly disappointed, as though he had supposed she had come on his account.

“Yes, my dear, drawing plans was quite a hobby of yours. Still, it was good to interrupt it for a while. Hobbies can run away with us, you know; we mustn’t allow that. We must hold the reins. I’ve never let anything run away with me; I’ve always pulled up. That’s what I tell Ladislaw. He’s like me, you know: likes to look into everything. We’re working on capital punishment. Ladislaw and I will accomplish a great deal together.”

“Yes,” said Dorothea with her usual directness. “Sir James tells me he hopes to see a great improvement in the way your estate is managed soon. You’re considering a valuation of the farms, repairs and better cottages, so that Tipton will become quite a different place. Oh, how wonderful!” She clasped her hands, recovering the eager, childlike manner marriage had subdued. “If I still lived here, I’d start riding again so I could go round with you and see it all! And Sir James says you’re going to employ Mr. Garth, who admired my cottages.”
“Chettam is a little premature, my dear,” said Mr. Brooke, colouring faintly. “Rather premature, you know. I never said I would do anything of the sort. Nor did I say I wouldn’t, you understand.”

“He’s simply sure you will,” Dorothea answered, her voice as clear and confident as a young chorister singing a creed, “because you intend to enter Parliament as someone concerned with improving people’s lives. And the condition of the land and the labourers must be among the first things improved. Think of Kit Downes, uncle, with his wife and seven children in a house whose only rooms are a sitting room and a bedroom scarcely bigger than this table! And the poor Dagleys in that collapsing farmhouse, living in the back kitchen and leaving the rest to the rats! That’s one reason I disliked the pictures here, dear uncle—the thing you thought so stupid of me. I used to return from the village carrying all its dirt and ugly harshness like a pain inside me. Then those simpering pictures in the drawing room seemed a wicked effort to enjoy something false while we ignored how hard reality was for our neighbours outside these walls. I don’t think we have any right to advocate wider improvements until we’ve tried to remedy the wrongs within our own reach.”

As she spoke, Dorothea grew more emotional, forgetting everything except the relief of letting her feelings pour out unchecked. That had once been a familiar experience, but since her marriage it had almost disappeared into a constant struggle between her energy and her fear. For the moment, Will’s admiration carried a chilling sense of distance. A man is seldom ashamed to feel that discovering greatness in a woman makes him love her less: nature, after all, meant greatness for men. Yet nature has sometimes made unfortunate mistakes in carrying out that intention. Good Mr. Brooke was a case in point. Under his niece’s eloquence, his masculine consciousness had become rather inarticulate. For a while the only expression he could find was to stand up, adjust his eyeglass and finger the papers before him. At last he spoke—

“There’s something in what you say, my dear, something in it—but not everything, eh, Ladislaw? You and I don’t care to hear our pictures and statues criticized. Young ladies are rather fervent, you know—a little one-sided, my dear. Art, poetry and so forth raise a nation—_emollit mores_—you understand some Latin now. But—eh? What is it?”
These last questions were directed to the footman, who had entered to report that the gamekeeper had caught one of Dagley’s boys holding a young hare he had just killed.
“I’m coming, I’m coming. I’ll let him off lightly, you know,” Mr. Brooke told Dorothea aside, shuffling away in quite a cheerful mood.
“I hope you see how right these changes are—the ones I, that is, Sir James wants,” Dorothea said to Will as soon as her uncle had left.

“I do, after hearing you speak. I won’t forget what you’ve said. But could you turn your thoughts to something else just now? I may not get another chance to tell you what has happened,” Will said. He rose impatiently and gripped the back of his chair with both hands.

“Please tell me,” Dorothea said anxiously. She too stood, going to the open window where Monk was peering in, panting and wagging his tail. Leaning against the window frame, she rested a hand on his head. For although, as we know, she disliked pets that had to be carried or were always underfoot, she respected dogs’ feelings and was invariably polite when she had to refuse their attentions.
Will followed her with his eyes alone. “I assume you know Mr. Casaubon has forbidden me to visit his house.”

“No, I didn’t,” Dorothea said after a pause, visibly distressed. “I’m very, very sorry,” she added sadly. She was remembering something Will knew nothing about: her conversation with her husband in the dark. Once more she despaired of influencing Mr. Casaubon’s conduct. But the particular look of her grief persuaded Will that it was not entirely for him personally, and that she had never imagined herself to be the cause of Mr. Casaubon’s dislike and jealousy. He felt a strange mixture of pleasure and frustration. He delighted in the thought that he could live, cherished and unsuspected, in the pure home of her mind, without limits on her kindness. Yet it vexed him that he mattered too little to her, that he was not dangerous enough: her unhesitating benevolence did nothing for his vanity. Still, his fear of any change in Dorothea outweighed his dissatisfaction, and when he spoke again he adopted a merely explanatory tone.

“Mr. Casaubon gives as his reason his disapproval of my taking a job here which he thinks beneath my standing as his cousin. I’ve told him I can’t yield on that point. It’s rather hard to expect my whole life to be obstructed by prejudices I consider ridiculous. Gratitude can be stretched until it becomes no better than a slave’s brand, stamped on us before we were old enough to understand it. I wouldn’t have accepted the position unless I intended to make it useful and honourable. I owe no other kind of consideration to the family’s dignity.”
Dorothea felt miserable. She believed her husband entirely wrong, for reasons beyond those Will had mentioned.
“Since you and Mr. Casaubon disagree, we had better not discuss it,” she said, with an unusual tremor in her voice. “You mean to stay?” She looked out over the lawn in sorrowful thought.
“Yes. But now I’ll scarcely ever see you,” Will said, his complaint sounding almost like a boy’s.
“No,” Dorothea replied, looking straight at him. “Scarcely ever. But I’ll hear about you. I’ll know what you’re doing for my uncle.”
“I’ll hear almost nothing about you,” said Will. “There’ll be no one to tell me.”
“Oh, my life is very simple,” said Dorothea. An exquisite smile curved her lips and lit up her sadness. “I’m always at Lowick.”
“What a dreadful prison,” Will exclaimed impulsively.
“No, you mustn’t think that,” said Dorothea. “I don’t long for anything.”

He said nothing, but some change in his face prompted her to continue. “For myself, I mean. Except that I wish I didn’t have so much more than my share while doing nothing for others. But I have a belief of my own that comforts me.”
“What belief?” asked Will, feeling rather jealous of it.

“That when we desire perfect goodness, even without quite knowing what it is, and without being able to do all we wish, we become part of the divine power resisting evil. We spread the edges of the light and reduce the ground on which darkness can fight.”
“That’s a beautiful form of mysticism—it’s a—”

“Please don’t give it a name,” said Dorothea, holding out her hands in appeal. “You’ll call it Persian, or attach some other place to it. It’s my life. I’ve discovered it for myself and can’t give it up. I’ve been discovering my religion ever since I was a little girl. I used to pray so much; now I hardly pray at all. I try not to want things just for myself, because they may not be good for other people, and I already have too much. I only told you so you would really understand how I spend my days at Lowick.”
“God bless you for telling me!” Will said fervently, a little surprised at himself. They looked at one another like two affectionate children sharing secrets about birds.
“What is your religion?” Dorothea asked. “I don’t mean what you know about religion. I mean the belief that gives you the most help.”
“To love goodness and beauty wherever I find them,” said Will. “But I’m rebellious. I don’t feel obliged, as you do, to submit to things I dislike.”
“But if what you like is good, it amounts to the same thing,” Dorothea said, smiling.
“Now you’re being subtle,” Will replied.

“Yes, Mr. Casaubon often tells me I’m too subtle. I never feel as though I am,” said Dorothea playfully. “But how long uncle is taking! I must find him. I really must get on to the Hall; Celia is waiting for me.”

Will offered to fetch Mr. Brooke. He soon appeared and said he would join Dorothea in the carriage as far as Dagley’s, where he wanted to speak about the young offender caught with the hare. During the drive Dorothea returned to the estate, but this time Mr. Brooke was prepared and took control of the conversation.

“Now, Chettam,” he answered, “finds fault with me, my dear. But I wouldn’t preserve game at all if it weren’t for him, and he can’t claim that expense benefits the tenants. It goes rather against my feelings. Poaching, for instance, if you examine it—I’ve often thought of taking up the subject. Not long ago Flavell, the Methodist preacher, was brought before us for knocking down a hare that crossed his path when he was out walking with his wife. Very quick he was; struck it on the neck.”
“I think that was very cruel,” Dorothea said.

“Well, I admit it seemed rather bad to me, coming from a Methodist preacher, you know. And Johnson said, ‘You can see what a hypo_crite_ he is.’ Really, Flavell hardly looked like ‘the highest style of man’—someone’s description of the Christian. Young, the poet Young, I think. You know Young? Well, there was Flavell in his shabby black gaiters, arguing that the Lord had sent him and his wife a good dinner and he had a right to knock it down, though he wasn’t a mighty hunter before the Lord like Nimrod. I assure you, it was quite comic. Fielding could have done something with it, or Scott—Scott might have worked it up. But when I really thought about it, I couldn’t help being pleased that the fellow should have a bit of hare to say grace over. It’s all prejudice—prejudice backed by the law, you know—about his stick and gaiters and so on. Still, reasoning about these things won’t do; the law’s the law. But I quieted Johnson and hushed it up. I suspect Chettam might have treated him more severely, yet he attacks me as if I were the hardest man in the county. Here we are at Dagley’s.”

Mr. Brooke stepped down at a gate into the farmyard, and Dorothea drove on. Things can look astonishingly uglier as soon as we suspect someone blames us for them. Even our own reflection may change after we hear a frank comment on its less attractive features. Conversely, it is remarkable how easily conscience tolerates our trespasses against people who never complain, or have no one to complain for them. Dagley’s farm had never looked so bleak to Mr. Brooke as it did today, with his mind smarting from the ‘Trumpet’s’ criticisms and Sir James’s repetition of them.

Of course, an observer under that softening spell of art which makes other people’s hardships picturesque might have been delighted by this farmstead, Freeman’s End. Dormer windows broke the old house’s dark red roof; ivy choked two chimneys; bundles of sticks blocked the wide porch. Half the windows were shut behind grey, worm-eaten shutters, around which jasmine branches tangled luxuriantly. The crumbling garden wall, with hollyhocks peering over it, offered a perfect study in mingled, muted colours. An elderly goat lay against the open back-kitchen door, no doubt kept for some interesting superstitious reason. The cowshed’s mossy thatch; the broken grey barn doors; the impoverished labourers in ragged breeches, almost finished unloading a wagon of grain for early threshing; the meagre dairy herd being tied up for milking, leaving half the shed brown and empty; even the pigs and white ducks wandering the neglected, uneven yard as if depressed by the thinness of the scraps they lived on—all this, under the gentle light of a sky marbled with high clouds, would have made the sort of picture we have all stopped to admire as “a charming little scene.” It would touch feelings quite different from those aroused by the agricultural depression and the miserable shortage of farming capital so often discussed in that period’s newspapers. But those troublesome connections were very much in Mr. Brooke’s mind just now, and spoiled the view. Mr. Dagley himself supplied a figure in the landscape, carrying a pitchfork and wearing his milking hat, a very old beaver hat flattened at the front. His coat and breeches were his best. He would not have worn them on a working day if he had not been to market and returned unusually late after treating himself to dinner at the Blue Bull’s communal table. Tomorrow he might wonder what had tempted him into such extravagance. Before dinner, though, something about the state of the country, the brief pause in harvesting before cutting the Far Dips, the stories about the new King and the handbills covering the walls had seemed to justify a little recklessness. Middlemarch took it as an unquestionable rule that good meat deserved good drink. Dagley understood this to mean plenty of ale with the meal, followed generously by rum and water. Those drinks contained at least this much truth: they could not lie enough to make poor Dagley cheerful. They merely loosened the tongue of his discontent. He had also swallowed too much muddled political talk, a stimulant dangerously unsettling to his farmer’s conservatism—the belief that everything as it stood was bad, and any change would probably make it worse. Flushed, his eyes fixed in an unmistakably quarrelsome stare, he stood gripping his pitchfork as his landlord approached with an easy shuffle, one hand in his trouser pocket, the other swinging a slender walking stick.
“Dagley, my good man,” Mr. Brooke began, aware of his own intention to be very kindly about the boy.

“Oh, so I’m a good man, am I? Thank you, sir, thank you,” Dagley replied with a loud, snarling sarcasm. Fag the sheepdog stirred and pricked up his ears, but on seeing Monk enter after lingering outside the yard, he sat down again to watch. “Glad to hear I’m such a good man.”

Mr. Brooke remembered that it was market day and supposed his worthy tenant had been dining. Still, he saw no reason not to proceed, provided he took the precaution of repeating his instructions to Mrs. Dagley.

“Your young Jacob was caught killing a young hare, Dagley. I’ve told Johnson to shut him in the empty stable for an hour or two, just to frighten him, you understand. He’ll be brought home before dark. You’ll keep an eye on him and tell him off, won’t you?”
“No, I won’t. I’ll be damned if I thrash my boy to please you or anyone else—not if you were twenty landlords instead of one, and a bad one at that.”

Dagley’s loud words brought his wife to the back-kitchen door, the house’s only entrance in use, which always stood open except in bad weather. “Well, well, I’ll speak to your wife. I didn’t mean a beating, you know,” Mr. Brooke said soothingly, and turned towards the house. But a gentleman walking away only strengthened Dagley’s determination to have his say. He followed immediately, with Fag slouching at his heels and sullenly dodging the small, probably well-meant approaches Monk was making.

“How are you, Mrs. Dagley?” Mr. Brooke asked rather hastily. “I’ve come about your boy. I don’t want you to beat him with a stick, you understand.” This time he took care to make himself perfectly clear.

Overworked Mrs. Dagley was a thin, worn woman whose life had been emptied of pleasure so completely that she had not even Sunday clothes to give her satisfaction in dressing for church. Since her husband’s return they had already quarrelled, and now she felt low and expected the worst. He answered before she could.

“No, and he won’t get a beating, whether you want it or not,” Dagley went on, hurling his voice as though he wanted it to strike a blow. “You’ve no business coming here talking about sticks when you won’t give a stick to mend the place. Go and ask in Middlemarch what they think of _your_ character.”

“You’d do better to keep quiet, Dagley,” his wife said, “instead of kicking over your own trough. When a man with a family has spent money at market and drunk too much, he’s done enough harm for one day. But I’d like to know what my boy’s done, sir.”

“Never you mind what he’s done,” Dagley said more fiercely. “It’s my place to speak, not yours. And I will speak. I’ll have my say, supper or no supper. What I say is, I’ve lived on your land, and my father and grandfather before me, and we’ve sunk our money into it. Me and my children might lie down and rot there to manure the ground we can’t afford to buy manure for, if the King wasn’t going to stop it.”
“My good man, you’re drunk, you know,” Mr. Brooke said in a confidential, but unwise, tone. “Another day, another day,” he added, starting to turn away.

Dagley immediately stepped in front of him. Fag growled low at his master’s heels as the man’s voice rose in volume and insult; Monk moved close too, keeping a dignified, silent watch. The labourers on the wagon had stopped to listen. Standing still seemed wiser than an absurd attempt to flee with a shouting man in pursuit.

“I’m no drunker than you, and not so much,” said Dagley. “I can hold my drink, and I know what I mean. I mean the King will put a stop to it. People who know say there’s to be a Reform, and landlords who’ve never done right by their tenants will get such treatment they’ll have to run for it. There are people in Middlemarch who know what this Reform is, and know who’ll have to run. They say, ‘We know who _your_ landlord is.’ I say, ‘I hope knowing him does you more good than it does me.’ They say, ‘He’s a tight-fisted one.’ ‘That he is,’ I say. ‘He supports Reform,’ they say. That’s what they told me. And I found out what Reform meant: sending you and your sort running, with some pretty strong-smelling things after you too. Do what you like now; I’m not afraid of you. You’d better leave my boy alone and look to yourself before Reform gets on your back. That’s what I have to say.” Mr. Dagley ended by driving his fork so firmly into the ground that he had trouble pulling it out again.

At this gesture Monk began barking loudly, giving Mr. Brooke a chance to escape. He left the yard as quickly as possible, astonished by the unfamiliar situation. No one had ever insulted him on his own land before. He had tended to think himself liked by everyone, as we all do when we think more about our own amiability than about what others may need from us. When he quarrelled with Caleb Garth twelve years earlier, he had supposed the tenants would welcome their landlord taking everything into his own hands.

Some readers following this account may marvel at the utter darkness of Mr. Dagley’s understanding. But in those days nothing was easier than for a farmer of his standing, working land his family had long held, to remain ignorant. Somehow this was possible despite a rector in the neighbouring parish who was a gentleman through and through, a nearer curate whose sermons were more learned than the rector’s, a landlord who had looked into everything, especially art and social improvement, and all the enlightenment of Middlemarch only three miles away. To see how easily human beings evade knowledge, try an ordinary acquaintance amid London’s intellectual blaze. Consider what that desirable dinner guest might have become if his education had consisted of a little arithmetic from Tipton’s parish clerk, and he could scarcely struggle through a Bible chapter because names such as Isaiah and Apollos defeated him even after spelling them out twice. Poor Dagley sometimes read a few verses on Sunday evening, and at least the world grew no darker for him. Some things he knew thoroughly: the sloppy farming habits and the contrary ways of weather, livestock and crops at Freeman’s End. Apparently that name was sarcastic. A man was free to leave if he liked, but nowhere on earth beyond it was open to him.

chapters.title: Book IV: Three Love Problems — Chapter XL
paragraphs:
Wise in his daily work was he:
To fruits of diligence,
And not to faiths or polity,
He plied his utmost sense.
These perfect in their little parts,
Whose work is all their prize—
Without them how could laws, or arts,
Or towered cities rise?

To trace effects, even those of an electric battery, we often have to change position and examine a particular combination or group some distance from where the movement began. The group I am approaching sits at Caleb Garth’s breakfast table, in the large parlour with the maps and desk: father, mother and five children. Mary was at home for the moment, waiting for a job. Christy, the next child after her, was getting inexpensive education and inexpensive meals in Scotland. To his father’s disappointment he had chosen books over that sacred calling, “business.”

The post had arrived: nine expensive letters, for which the postman had been paid three shillings and twopence. Mr. Garth forgot his tea and toast as he read them and laid them open, one on top of another. Sometimes he slowly shook his head; sometimes he pursed his lips in silent argument. He did remember, though, to cut off a large red seal intact, and Letty seized it like an eager terrier.
The others talked freely around him. Nothing interrupted Caleb’s concentration except someone shaking the table while he was writing.

Two of the nine letters were Mary’s. She read them, handed them to her mother and sat absently playing with her teaspoon. Then, suddenly remembering it, she returned to the sewing she had kept in her lap throughout breakfast.
“Oh, don’t sew, Mary!” said Ben, pulling down her arm. “Make a peacock out of this bread for me.” He had been kneading a small lump ready for the purpose.

“No, you little mischief!” Mary answered cheerfully, giving his hand a light prick with her needle. “Try shaping it yourself. You’ve watched me often enough. I must finish this sewing. It’s for Rosamond Vincy: she’s getting married next week and can’t possibly marry without this handkerchief.” The last idea amused Mary, and she finished with a laugh.
“Why can’t she, Mary?” asked Letty, deeply interested in the mystery. She brought her head so close that Mary now pointed the threatening needle at her nose.
“Because it belongs to a set of twelve, and without it there would only be eleven,” Mary explained solemnly. Letty settled back, feeling she had learned something.
“Have you decided, my dear?” Mrs. Garth asked, putting the letters down.
“I’ll go to the school in York,” Mary said. “I’m better suited to teaching in a school than in a private family. I prefer classes. And I have to teach, you see; there’s nothing else available.”
“To me, teaching seems the most delightful work there is,” said Mrs. Garth, with a hint of reproach. “I could understand your objection if you didn’t know enough, Mary, or if you disliked children.”

“I suppose we never quite understand why someone dislikes what we enjoy, mother,” Mary answered rather shortly. “I’m not fond of classrooms. I prefer the world outside. It’s a very inconvenient fault of mine.”
“It must be terribly dull, always being in a girls’ school,” said Alfred. “All those idiots, like Mrs. Ballard’s pupils walking in pairs.”
“And none of their games are worth playing,” Jim added. “They can’t throw or jump. I’m not surprised Mary doesn’t like it.”
“What doesn’t Mary like, eh?” their father asked, looking over his spectacles and pausing before opening the next letter.
“Being surrounded by silly girls,” Alfred answered.
“Is it the job you heard about, Mary?” Caleb asked gently, looking at his daughter.
“Yes, father, at the school in York. I’ve decided to accept. It’s certainly the best offer. Thirty-five pounds a year, with extra for teaching the youngest piano strummers.”
“Poor child! I wish we could keep her here with us, Susan,” Caleb said, looking sorrowfully at his wife.
“Mary couldn’t be happy if she neglected her duty,” Mrs. Garth pronounced, conscious of having fulfilled her own.
“Doing such a nasty duty wouldn’t make me happy,” Alfred said. Mary and her father laughed silently, but Mrs. Garth replied with seriousness—
“Please find a better word than ‘nasty,’ my dear Alfred, for all the things you happen to dislike. And suppose the money Mary earns helps send you to Mr. Hanmer’s school?”
“I think that would be a great shame. But she’s a splendid old girl,” Alfred said, getting up and tilting Mary’s head back to kiss her.

Mary blushed and laughed, but could not hide her rising tears. Watching over his spectacles, his eyebrows drooping at the corners, Caleb looked both delighted and sad before returning to his letter. Even Mrs. Garth, whose lips curved in quiet satisfaction, let the unsuitable language go uncorrected. Ben immediately picked it up, singing, “She’s a splendid old girl, old girl, old girl!” to a galloping rhythm which he beat out with his fist on Mary’s arm.

Now Mrs. Garth’s attention shifted to her husband, who was already deeply absorbed in the letter he had just opened. His expression of serious surprise worried her a little. But he disliked being interrupted with questions while reading, so she continued to watch anxiously until a small, delighted laugh suddenly shook him. Turning back to the beginning of the letter, he looked at her over his spectacles and said in a low voice, “What do you think, Susan?”

She stood behind him and placed a hand on his shoulder while they read the letter together. Sir James Chettam was offering Mr. Garth the management of the family estates at Freshitt and elsewhere. He added that Mr. Brooke of Tipton had asked him to find out whether Mr. Garth would also be willing to resume managing the Tipton property. In very courteous terms, Sir James explained that he particularly wished to see Freshitt and Tipton under one management. He hoped to show that the two appointments could be combined on terms Mr. Garth would find agreeable, and would be pleased to see him at the Hall at noon the following day.

“That’s a generous letter, isn’t it, Susan?” Caleb said, looking up at his wife. She moved her hand from his shoulder to his ear and rested her chin on his head. “I can see Brooke didn’t like to ask me himself,” he went on, laughing silently.

“This is an honour for your father, children,” Mrs. Garth said, turning to the five pairs of eyes fixed on their parents. “The people who dismissed him years ago are asking him to return. It proves he did his work so well that they miss him.”
“Like Cincinnatus—hooray!” Ben cried, rocking astride his chair in comfortable confidence that the usual rules had been suspended.
“Will they come and fetch him, mother?” Letty asked, picturing the Mayor and Corporation in their ceremonial robes.
Mrs. Garth smiled and patted Letty’s head. But her husband was gathering his letters, about to retreat beyond reach into the sanctuary called “business.” She pressed his shoulder and spoke firmly—
“Now, Caleb, make sure you ask for proper pay.”

“Oh, certainly,” Caleb replied in a deep tone of agreement, as if no one could reasonably have expected otherwise. “Together they’ll bring in between four and five hundred.” Then he gave a small start of recollection. “Mary, write and turn down the school. Stay here and help your mother. Now I’ve thought of that, I’m as pleased as Punch.”

No one’s manner could have resembled the triumphant Punch less than Caleb’s. But finding phrases was not his talent, although he took great care over his letters and regarded his wife as a storehouse of correct expression.

The children were almost in uproar now. Mary held her cambric embroidery towards her mother, pleading for it to be rescued while the boys dragged her into a dance. Serenely happy, Mrs. Garth began collecting the cups and plates. Caleb pushed his chair back as though intending to go to his desk, but remained seated with his letters in his hand. He looked thoughtfully at the floor, stretching the fingers of his left hand in a silent language of his own. At last he spoke—

“It’s a terrible pity Christy didn’t take to business, Susan. I’ll need help before long. And Alfred must go off to engineering; I’ve settled that.” He returned for a moment to thought and gesturing fingers, then continued. “I’ll make Brooke draw up new agreements with the tenants, and I’ll work out a crop rotation. I’d wager we can make excellent bricks from the clay at Bott’s corner. I must investigate; it would cut the repair costs. It’s a wonderful piece of work, Susan! A man without a family would be happy to do it for nothing.”
“Take care you don’t,” said his wife, raising a warning finger.

“No, no. But once a man understands the nature of the work, it’s a wonderful opportunity: to put a piece of the country in good condition, as they say, guide people into farming properly, and carry out some sound planning and solid building that will benefit both the living and those who come after them. I’d rather have that than a fortune. I believe it’s the most honourable work there is.” Caleb put down his letters, slipped his fingers between his waistcoat buttons and sat upright. Then, slowly turning his head aside, he continued with awe in his voice. “It’s a great gift from God, Susan.”

“It is indeed, Caleb,” his wife answered with matching warmth. “And your children will be blessed to have had a father who did such work, whose good work lasts even when his name has been forgotten.” After that, she could say no more about his pay.

That evening Caleb sat quietly, tired from his day’s work, his notebook open on his knee. Mrs. Garth and Mary were sewing, and Letty sat in a corner whispering a conversation with her doll, when Mr. Farebrother came along the orchard path. With the clumps of grass and apple branches, he shared the bright August patches of light and shadow. We know he liked the Garths, his parishioners, and had thought Mary worth mentioning to Lydgate. He made full use of a clergyman’s privilege to ignore Middlemarch’s social distinctions, and always told his mother that Mrs. Garth was more of a lady than any married woman in town. Yet, you see, he spent his evenings at the Vincys’, where the lady of the house, though less of a lady, offered a brightly lit drawing room and whist. In those days, respect was not the sole basis of social life. Nevertheless, the Vicar sincerely respected the Garths, and the family found nothing surprising in his visit. Even so, he explained it while still shaking hands. “I’m here as a messenger, Mrs. Garth. I have something to tell you and Garth on Fred Vincy’s behalf. The truth is, poor fellow,” he continued, sitting down and turning his bright eyes on his three listeners, “he’s been confiding in me.”
Mary’s heart began beating faster. She wondered how much Fred had confided.
“We haven’t seen him for months,” Caleb said. “I couldn’t imagine what had become of the lad.”

“He’s been away visiting,” the Vicar explained. “Home had grown a little too uncomfortable, and Lydgate told his mother he wasn’t fit to start studying yet. But yesterday he came and poured out all his troubles. I’m very glad he did. I’ve watched him grow up since he was fourteen, and I’m so much at home in their house that the children feel like my own nephews and nieces. Still, it isn’t easy to advise him. He asked me to tell you he’s going away. He feels so wretched about owing you money and being unable to repay it that he can’t bear to come himself, even to say goodbye.”
“Tell him it doesn’t matter a farthing,” said Caleb, waving a hand. “We felt the pinch and got through it. And now I’m going to be as rich as a Jew.”
“By which he means,” Mrs. Garth explained, smiling at the Vicar, “we’ll have enough to bring up the boys properly and let Mary stay at home.”
“What treasure have you found?” Mr. Farebrother asked.

“I’m to manage two estates, Freshitt and Tipton, perhaps with a nice little piece of land at Lowick as well. They’re all connected by family, and once work starts flowing it spreads like water. It makes me very happy, Mr. Farebrother”—Caleb leaned his head back a little and spread his arms along the chair arms—“to have another chance at letting land and putting one or two ideas for improvements into practice. As I’ve often told Susan, it’s dreadfully frustrating to sit on horseback looking over a hedge at something done wrong, without being able to put your hand to it and make it right. I can’t imagine how people in politics bear it. Seeing a few hundred acres badly managed is enough to drive me nearly mad.”
Caleb rarely volunteered such a long speech. But happiness worked on him like mountain air: his eyes shone, and the words came easily.

“My warmest congratulations, Garth,” said the Vicar. “I couldn’t have better news to take Fred Vincy. He spoke a great deal about the harm he’d done by making you part with money you needed for other things—robbing you of it, he called it. I wish Fred weren’t such an idle fellow. He has some very good qualities, and his father treats him a little harshly.”
“Where is he going?” Mrs. Garth asked somewhat coldly.

“He intends to try for his degree again, and he’s going up before term to study. That was my advice. I’m not urging him into the Church; quite the opposite. But if he goes and works hard enough to pass, he’ll at least prove he has some determination and energy. He’s completely adrift and has no idea what else to do. This much will satisfy his father. Meanwhile, I’ve promised to try to reconcile Vincy to his son choosing a different career. Fred freely admits he isn’t suited to being a clergyman, and I’d do all I could to stop anyone taking the disastrous step of choosing the wrong profession. He repeated something you said, Miss Garth. Do you remember it?” Mr. Farebrother once called her “Mary,” but his tact now led him to show her greater respect precisely because, in Mrs. Vincy’s words, she worked for her bread.
Mary felt uneasy but determined to take it lightly. She answered at once, “I’ve said so many rude things to Fred. We’ve been playmates for so long.”
“According to him, you said he would be one of those absurd clergymen who make the whole profession look absurd. It was such a sharp remark that I felt a little of its edge myself.”
Caleb laughed with enjoyment. “She gets that tongue from you, Susan.”
“Not the flippant part, father,” Mary said quickly, afraid her mother might be offended. “It’s rather unfair of Fred to repeat my flippant remarks to Mr. Farebrother.”

“It certainly was a rash thing to say, my dear,” said Mrs. Garth, who regarded speaking ill of authority as a serious offence. “A ridiculous curate in the next parish wouldn’t make us value our own Vicar less.”

“Still, there’s something in her point,” said Caleb, unwilling to see Mary’s shrewdness dismissed. “One bad workman makes people distrust others in his trade. Things are connected,” he added, looking down and shifting his feet uncomfortably, feeling that he had more thoughts than words to express them.

“Certainly,” the Vicar said, amused. “When we behave contemptibly, we tune other people’s minds to contempt. I agree with Miss Garth, whether her view condemns me or not. As for Fred Vincy, though, fairness requires a little allowance. Old Featherstone helped spoil him by raising false expectations. There was something positively devilish in leaving him nothing in the end. But Fred has enough good taste not to dwell on it. What troubles him most is having offended you, Mrs. Garth. He thinks you’ll never have a good opinion of him again.”
“Fred has disappointed me,” Mrs. Garth said firmly. “But when he gives me good reason, I’ll be ready to think well of him again.”
At this point Mary left the room, taking little Letty along with her.

“Oh, we must forgive young people when they’re sorry,” Caleb said, watching Mary shut the door. “And you’re right, Mr. Farebrother, that old man had the devil in him. Now Mary’s out of the room, I must tell you something. Only Susan and I know, and you mustn’t repeat it. The old scoundrel wanted Mary to burn one of his wills the very night he died, when she was sitting up alone with him. He offered her some money from the box beside him if she’d do it. But Mary couldn’t possibly do such a thing, you understand. She wouldn’t touch his iron chest, or anything of that sort. Now, the will he wanted burnt was the latest one. If Mary had obeyed him, Fred Vincy would have received ten thousand pounds. The old man did turn back towards him at the very end. Poor Mary feels that deeply. She couldn’t help it, and she acted rightly, but she says it feels like knocking down someone’s property and accidentally breaking it while properly defending yourself. Somehow I feel it with her. Instead of holding a grudge for the harm the poor lad did us, I’d gladly make it up to him if I could. What do you think, sir? Susan disagrees. She says—tell him what you say, Susan.”
“Mary couldn’t have acted differently, even if she had known how it would affect Fred,” said Mrs. Garth, stopping her work and looking at Mr. Farebrother.
“And she knew nothing about it. I don’t think another person’s loss should burden our conscience when it results from our doing what is right.”

The Vicar did not answer at once. “It’s the feeling,” Caleb said. “The child feels that way, and I feel it with her. You don’t intend your horse to step on a dog when you’re backing out of someone’s way. But once it happens, it goes straight through you.”

“I’m sure Mrs. Garth would agree with that,” said Mr. Farebrother, who for some reason seemed more inclined to reflect than to talk. “I could hardly call the feeling you describe towards Fred wrong—or rather, mistaken. Though no man has the right to demand such a feeling from anyone.”
“Well, well,” Caleb said, “it’s a secret. You won’t tell Fred.”
“Of course not. But I will take him the other good news: that you can afford the loss he caused.”

Mr. Farebrother left soon afterwards. Seeing Mary and Letty in the orchard, he went over to say goodbye. They made a lovely picture in the western light, which brightened the apples on the old, sparsely leaved branches. Mary, wearing lavender gingham with black ribbons, held a basket; Letty, in her worn yellow cotton, gathered windfalls. If you want a more precise idea of Mary’s appearance, the odds are you will see a face like hers tomorrow in a crowded street, provided you watch for it. She will not be among those daughters of Zion who walk proudly, with necks stretched high, wandering eyes and mincing steps. Let them pass. Look instead for a small, plump, brownish young woman whose bearing is steady but quiet, who looks about her without imagining anyone is looking at her. If she has a broad face, a square forehead, distinct eyebrows and dark curly hair, with amusement in her eyes that her mouth keeps secret, while the rest of her features are quite unremarkable, take that ordinary but agreeable person as Mary Garth’s portrait. Make her smile and you would see perfect little teeth. Make her angry and she would keep her voice low, but probably say something as bitter as anything you had ever tasted. Show her kindness and she would remember it for ever. Mary admired the handsome little Vicar, with his keen face and carefully brushed, threadbare clothes, more than any man she had known. She had never heard him say anything foolish, although she knew he did unwise things. Perhaps foolish remarks offended her more than any of his imprudent actions. At any rate, it was striking that the Vicar’s actual failings as a clergyman never seemed to provoke the scorn and dislike she already felt for Fred Vincy’s imagined future failings in that role. Such inconsistencies, I imagine, occur in minds more mature than Mary Garth’s. We reserve our impartiality for abstract merit and fault, neither of which any of us has ever met. Can anyone guess which of these very different men called out her particular womanly tenderness: the one she was most ready to criticize, or the other?

“Do you have a message for your old playmate, Miss Garth?” the Vicar asked. He took a fragrant apple from the basket she offered and slipped it into his pocket. “Something to soften that severe verdict? I’m going directly to see him.”
“No,” Mary said, smiling and shaking her head. “If I said he wouldn’t be ridiculous as a clergyman, I would have to say he’d be worse than ridiculous. But I’m very glad he’s going away to work.”

“And I’m very glad _you_ aren’t going away to work. I’m sure my mother would be delighted if you came to visit her at the vicarage. You know how she enjoys talking to young people, and she has a great deal to tell about the past. You really would be doing her a kindness.”

“I’d love to, if I may,” Mary said. “Everything has become too happy all at once. I thought longing for home would always be part of my life. Without that grievance I feel rather empty. Perhaps it filled my mind in place of sense?”

“May I come too, Mary?” Letty whispered. She was a most inconvenient child, listening to everything. But Mr. Farebrother sent her into delight by pinching her chin and kissing her cheek, an event she later reported to both her parents.

Anyone watching the Vicar closely as he walked towards Lowick might have noticed him shrug twice. I think the few Englishmen who use that gesture are never of a heavy nature—or, for fear of some ponderous exception, hardly ever. Usually they have sensitive temperaments and considerable tolerance for people’s smaller faults, including their own. The Vicar was conducting an inward conversation. He told himself that Fred and Mary probably felt more for each other than the affection of childhood playmates. Then he asked in reply whether this young woman was not far too fine for that unformed young gentleman. His answer was the first shrug. Next he laughed at himself for apparently feeling jealous, as though he were in a position to marry. “Which,” he added, “as any balance sheet would plainly show, I am not.” That produced the second shrug.

What could two such different men see in this “brown patch,” as Mary called herself? Certainly her lack of beauty was not the attraction. And let all plain young women beware of society’s dangerous encouragement to put their trust in being plain. In our old nation, a human being is a marvellous whole, slowly formed through a long exchange of influences. Charm arises between two such wholes: the person who loves and the person who is loved.
Later, when he and his wife were alone, Caleb said, “Susan, guess what’s on my mind.”
“Crop rotation,” Mrs. Garth replied, smiling at him over her knitting, “or perhaps the back doors of the cottages at Tipton.”

“No,” Caleb said seriously. “I’m thinking I could be a great help to Fred Vincy. Christy’s gone, Alfred will soon be gone, and Jim won’t be ready to start work for another five years. I’ll need help. Fred could join me, learn how things work and assist me. If he gives up the idea of being a parson, it might turn him into a useful man. What do you think?”
“I think his family would object to that almost more than to any other honest occupation,” Mrs. Garth replied decisively.

“Why should I care if they object?” Caleb said, showing the firmness that came over him when he had settled an opinion. “The lad is an adult and must earn his living. He has enough sense and is quick enough. He likes being on the land, and I believe he could learn the work well if he applied himself.”

“But would he? His parents wanted to make a fine gentleman of him, and I think he feels much the same himself. They all consider us beneath them. And if you made the offer, I’m sure Mrs. Vincy would say we wanted to get Fred for Mary.”
“Life’s a sorry business if nonsense like that is to decide it,” Caleb said with disgust.
“Yes, but some kinds of pride are proper, Caleb.”

“To me it’s improper pride that lets foolish notions stop you doing something good. No kind of work,” Caleb said fervently, extending a hand and moving it up and down for emphasis, “could ever be done well if you listened to what fools say. You must know inside yourself that your plan is right, and then follow it.”

“I won’t oppose a plan once you’ve set your heart on it, Caleb,” Mrs. Garth said. She was a firm woman, but knew that on certain points her gentle husband was firmer still. “Even so, Fred seems definitely to be returning to college. Wouldn’t it be better to wait and see what he chooses afterwards? It’s hard to keep people at something against their will. And you aren’t quite certain yet about your own position, or how much help you’ll need.”

“Well, perhaps we should wait a little. But I’m fairly sure I’ll have enough work for two. I’ve always had my hands full of odds and ends, and new things are always coming along. Why, just yesterday—goodness, I don’t think I told you!—two different men approached me about the very same valuation. Rather odd. Who do you think they were?” Caleb took a pinch of snuff and held it between his fingers as though it formed part of his explanation. He liked a pinch when he remembered it, but usually forgot he had that pleasure available.
His wife lowered her knitting and gave him her attention.
“Well, that Rigg fellow—Rigg Featherstone—was one. But Bulstrode asked first, so I’ll be doing it for him. I can’t yet tell whether they’re arranging a mortgage or a sale.”
“Surely the man isn’t going to sell the land he’s only just inherited—the land he took the name for?” Mrs. Garth asked.

“The devil knows,” Caleb replied. He never referred knowledge of discreditable conduct to any higher authority than the devil. “But I do know Bulstrode has wanted to get hold of a fine piece of land for a long time. And land is hard to come by in this part of the country.”

Instead of taking his snuff, Caleb carefully scattered it. Then he added, “Things take curious turns. There’s this land everyone expected Fred to get, though apparently the old man never meant him to have a foot of it. Instead he left it to that illegitimate son he’d kept secret, expecting him to stay there and annoy everybody as thoroughly as he could have done himself if he’d managed to live. I say, wouldn’t it be curious if Bulstrode got it after all? The old man hated him and would never use his bank.”
“Why would the miserable creature hate a man he had nothing to do with?” Mrs. Garth asked.

“Pah! What’s the use of asking why such fellows do things? The human soul,” Caleb said, lowering his voice and gravely shaking his head as he always did with that phrase, “the human soul, once thoroughly rotten, will grow every kind of poisonous toadstool, and no eye can discover where the seed came from.”

It was one of Caleb’s peculiarities that, struggling to find words for his thoughts, he caught at fragments of language associated in his mind with particular attitudes or feelings. Whenever he felt awe, a suggestion of biblical language haunted him, although he could scarcely have produced an exact quotation.
